body:
That's interesting. We thought we address this issue in 4.0.26. (See `AbstractChannelHandlerContext.fireChannelReadComplete()` calls `ctx.read()` automatically to prevent the stall like you mentioned.)

Would you mind if I ask you to write a simple reproducer?  You could take a look at `SocketSslEchoTest` and write something similar.

@trustin I read the codes you mentioned and found steps of this problem. 
1. SslHandler decodes packets and call next.fireChannelRead()
   - At this time, invokeNextChannelRead of SslHandler context is true, and invokePrevRead is false.
2. The next handler handles channelRead() and call Channel.read() before returning it.
   - At this time, invokePrevRead of SslHandler context becomes true.
3. SslHandler handles channelReadComplete().
   - At this time, the flags are changed to false by the following codes.
     
       if (invokedNextChannelRead ||  // The handler of this context produced a message, or
           !invokedThisChannelRead) { // it is not required to produce a message to trigger the event.
     
     ```
       invokedNextChannelRead = false;
       invokedPrevRead = false;
     ```
4. SslHandler handles channelRead(). But SslHandler cannot call next.fireChannelRead() because it does not have the whole encrypted packets. (I mentioned above)
   - At this time, there is no change of the flags of SslHandler context.
5. SslHandler handles channelReadComplete(). Channel.read() will not be called because invokePrevRead of context is false. Refer to the following codes.
   
   ```
   /**
    * At this point, we are sure the handler of this context did not produce anything and
    * we suppressed the {@code channelReadComplete()} event.
    *
    * If the next handler invoked {@link #read()} to read something but nothing was produced
    * by the handler of this context, someone has to issue another {@link #read()} operation
    * until the handler of this context produces something.
    *
    * Why? Because otherwise the next handler will not receive {@code channelRead()} nor
    * {@code channelReadComplete()} event at all for the {@link #read()} operation it issued.
    */
   if (invokedPrevRead && !channel().config().isAutoRead()) {
       /**
        * The next (or upstream) handler invoked {@link #read()}, but it didn't get any
        * {@code channelRead()} event. We should read once more, so that the handler of the current
        * context have a chance to produce something.
        */
       read();
   } else {
       invokedPrevRead = false;
   }
   ```
6. After that, no more channelRead() will be called.

Could you review the steps I found? I will try to write a simple reproducer later.
Didn't have time for taking a close look yet, but I didn't forget about this.

https://github.com/hyangtack/netty/commit/b52bac04c0f8b49cb10079783132dabf1768ad99

@trustin Could you take a look at this commit? Should I call ctx.read at channelReadComplete?  When I moved it to channelReadComplete, tests succeeded. Please let me know if I'm wrong.

@hyangtack Thanks for the detailed analysis. The expected user behavior was to call `ctx.read()` at `channelReadComplete()`, but it should work even if `ctx.read()` was called at `channelRead()`. So, yeah, the workaround in your case would be to move `ctx.read()` from `channelRead()` to `channelReadComplete()`.
@hyangtack Please stay tuned. I'm working on a fix.

issue.title: 4.1.0-Beta4: Regression in HttpRequestDecoder

repository.name: netty
repository.description: Netty project - an event-driven asynchronous network application framework

issue.body:
We recently noticed that one of our Netty services was intermittently ignoring requests, causing the caller to timeout. Adding LoggingHandlers all over the place revealed that the failing request was received but never made it out of HttpRequestDecoder.

The connection is reused by the client and saw multiple similar requests before the server somehow choked on the last one. The server uses autoRead=false in case that is relevant.

We promptly reverted to 4.1.0-Beta3 and this failure mode completely disappeared. A quick look at the commit log between the two tags show a significant refactor of HttpRequestDecoder and some more subtle changes to ByteToMessageDecoder which are probably responsible for the regression.
